currents.name: Gulf Stream
currents.desc: A fast river of warm tropical water that flows north along the U.S. East Coast, then turns toward Europe.
effects: Warm water heats and moistens the air above it. This fuels storms that run up the East Coast.
It keeps winters milder along the coast than farther inland.
Where it meets the cold Labrador Current, thick fog forms.

currents.name: North Atlantic Drift
currents.desc: The Gulf Stream’s slower continuation across the North Atlantic toward Europe.
effects: It carries warmth to northwest Europe. London and Bergen are far milder in winter than places at the same latitude in Canada.
Ports in Norway stay free of ice all winter.

currents.name: Norwegian Current
currents.desc: Warm water flowing north along the coast of Norway.
effects: Keeps the Norwegian coast much milder than other places so far north.
Warm, moist air from the sea brings heavy rain and snow to the mountains of western Norway.

currents.name: Labrador Current
currents.desc: Cold water flowing south from the Arctic along Labrador and Newfoundland.
effects: Cools the air, so Newfoundland and Labrador are cold and foggy.
Carries icebergs south into shipping lanes.
Meets the warm Gulf Stream near the Grand Banks, which makes some of the foggiest water in the world.

currents.name: East Greenland Current
currents.desc: Cold, icy water flowing south along the east coast of Greenland.
effects: Keeps the air near Greenland’s east coast very cold.
Carries sea ice south.

currents.name: Canary Current
currents.desc: Cool water flowing south along Portugal and northwest Africa.
effects: Cools the coastal air, so the coast is cooler and drier than inland.
Helps make the Sahara’s Atlantic coast a desert.
Gives the Canary Islands mild temperatures all year.

currents.name: North Equatorial Current
currents.desc: Warm water pushed west near the equator by the trade winds.
effects: Stores heat in the tropics and carries it west.
Feeds the Gulf Stream (Atlantic) and the Kuroshio (Pacific).

currents.name: South Equatorial Current
currents.desc: Warm water pushed west along and just south of the equator by the trade winds.
effects: Piles warm water against the western side of the ocean basins.
Feeds the Brazil and East Australian Currents.

currents.name: Brazil Current
currents.desc: Warm water flowing south along the coast of Brazil.
effects: Warms the air along southeastern Brazil, adding humidity and rain.
Meets the cold Falkland Current off Argentina.

currents.name: Falkland (Malvinas) Current
currents.desc: Cold water flowing north along the coast of Argentina.
effects: Cools the air over Patagonia and eastern Argentina.
Brings fog where it meets the warm Brazil Current.

currents.name: Benguela Current
currents.desc: Cold water flowing north along the coast of southwest Africa.
effects: Cools the air so much that little rain falls. This helps make the Namib Desert.
Fog is common along the coast.
Cool air, cool water and strong winds make Cape Town’s Atlantic side chilly even in summer.

currents.name: Agulhas Current
currents.desc: A strong, warm current flowing south along the southeast coast of Africa.
effects: Warm water brings humid air and rain to southeastern Africa.
Where it meets strong winds and waves near the Cape, it can make dangerous seas.

currents.name: Antarctic Circumpolar Current
currents.desc: The largest current: cold water circling Antarctica from west to east.
effects: Keeps Antarctica cold by cutting it off from warmer water.
Strong westerly winds blow over it (the “Roaring Forties” and “Furious Fifties”), so the Southern Ocean is stormy.

currents.name: West Australian Current
currents.desc: Cool water flowing north off the west coast of Australia.
effects: Cools coastal air.
Contributes to dry weather on Australia’s west and northwest coast.

currents.name: East Australian Current
currents.desc: Warm water flowing south along the east coast of Australia.
effects: Warms the air along the east coast, adding humidity and rain.
Makes the coast warmer in winter than the same latitude on the west coast.

currents.name: Kuroshio Current
currents.desc: The Pacific’s version of the Gulf Stream: warm water flowing north past Japan.
effects: Warms southern Japan, giving it a mild, humid climate.
Warm water helps feed typhoons and strong storms near Japan.

currents.name: Oyashio Current
currents.desc: Cold water flowing south from the Bering Sea past Kamchatka and the Kuril Islands.
effects: Cools northern Japan.
Where it meets the warm Kuroshio, fog is common.

currents.name: North Pacific Current
currents.desc: The Kuroshio’s water drifting east across the North Pacific.
effects: Carries mild water toward North America.
Splits into the cold California Current and the warm Alaska Current.

currents.name: Alaska Current
currents.desc: Relatively warm water flowing north and west along the coast of southern Alaska.
effects: Keeps southern Alaska’s coast milder and wetter than other places at that latitude.
Moist, mild air meeting coastal mountains brings heavy rain and snow.

currents.name: California Current
currents.desc: Cool water flowing south along the west coast of North America.
effects: Cools the air, giving San Francisco cool, foggy summers.
Makes summers dry along the coast.
Cold water rising from below (upwelling) makes the sea rich in life.

currents.name: Peru (Humboldt) Current
currents.desc: Cold water flowing north along the west coast of South America.
effects: Cools the air so much that it rarely rains. The Atacama Desert lies next to it.
Lima is cloudy and foggy but very dry.
Cold, nutrient-rich water makes this one of the richest fishing areas on Earth.
